key_terms.meaning: Binary ASK with zero amplitude for bit 0: s(t) = A·b(t)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t); average E<sub>b</sub> = A²T<sub>b</sub>/4; coherent P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)).
h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub> = |f<sub>1</sub> − f<sub>0</sub>|/R<sub>b</sub>; Carson bandwidth B ≈ 2(Δf + R<sub>b</sub>).
nR<sub>b</sub>/2 for coherent and nR<sub>b</sub> for non-coherent detection (n a positive whole number).
s(t) = ±√(2E<sub>b</sub>/T<sub>b</sub>)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t); points ±√E<sub>b</sub>; P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) = ½erfc(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)).
Q(x) = P(Z > x) for a standard normal Z; Q(x) = ½erfc(x/√2).
d<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ d<sub>k−1</sub>; data in the phase change; P<sub>b</sub> = ½e<sup>−E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub></sup>.
Envelope detectors at f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>0</sub>; spacing ≥ R<sub>b</sub>; P<sub>b</sub> = ½e<sup>−E<sub>b</sub>/2N<sub>0</sub></sup>.
Two bits per symbol, R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2, B = R<sub>b</sub> (rectangular), P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)).
d = 2√E<sub>s</sub> sin(π/M); P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 2Q(√(2E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)·sin(π/M)); η = k/2.
M orthogonal tones; B ≈ M·R<sub>s</sub>/2 (coherent); P<sub>s</sub> ≤ (M − 1)Q(√(E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)).
√M levels per axis; E<sub>s</sub> = 2(M − 1)a²/3; P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 4(1 − 1/√M)Q(√(3E<sub>s</sub>/((M − 1)N<sub>0</sub>))).
CPFSK with h = 0.5: tones f<sub>c</sub> ± R<sub>b</sub>/4; phase changes ±90° per bit; main lobe 1.5R<sub>b</sub>.
Gaussian filter before MSK; B = (BT)·R<sub>b</sub>; GSM uses BT = 0.3.
Smallest distance between constellation points; P<sub>s</sub> ≲ N<sub>nb</sub>·Q(d<sub>min</sub>/√(2N<sub>0</sub>)).
η = R<sub>b</sub>/B in b/s/Hz: k/2 with rectangular pulses, k with ideal Nyquist pulses.
Main lobes: BPSK 2R<sub>b</sub>, QPSK R<sub>b</sub>, MSK 1.5R<sub>b</sub>; MSK side lobes −23 dB, falling as 1/f⁴.
DSSS: G<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>c</sub>/R<sub>b</sub> chips per bit; FHSS: G<sub>p</sub> ≈ number of hop channels.
M<sub>j</sub> = G<sub>p</sub>(dB) − (E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)<sub>req</sub>(dB) − L<sub>sys</sub>(dB).
Shift-register PN code of period 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 with balance, run and two-valued autocorrelation properties.
Δf = 1/T<sub>u</sub>; IFFT builds, FFT separates; Y[k] = H[k]X[k] + W[k].
Copy of the symbol's tail, T<sub>cp</sub> ≥ τ<sub>max</sub>; T = T<sub>u</sub> + T<sub>cp</sub>.
B<sub>c</sub> ≈ 1/(5σ<sub>τ</sub>); f<sub>d</sub> = vf<sub>c</sub>/c; T<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.423/f<sub>d</sub>.

takeaways: OOK switches the carrier on and off and BFSK switches its frequency; both have P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) coherently, 3 dB worse than BPSK, and BFSK tones must be spaced by a whole multiple of R<sub>b</sub>/2 (coherent) or R<sub>b</sub> (non-coherent).
BPSK's antipodal points are 2√E<sub>b</sub> apart, giving P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)), the best binary result: 9.6 dB for 10<sup>−5.</sup>
Non-coherent BFSK and DPSK need no carrier phase and cost under 1 dB at 10<sup>−5</sup>; DPSK puts the data in the phase change, so a 180° slip does no harm.
QPSK carries two bits per symbol in the bandwidth of one with BPSK's P<sub>b</sub>; M-ary PSK saves more bandwidth but its points close in as 2√E<sub>s</sub> sin(π/M).
M-ary FSK spends bandwidth to save power; QAM spends power and linearity to save bandwidth.
MSK is CPFSK with h = 0.5: tones f<sub>c</sub> ± R<sub>b</sub>/4, a continuous phase trellis, BPSK error rate and side lobes falling as 1/f⁴; GMSK narrows it further at the cost of ISI.
d<sub>min</sub> sets the error rate and M sets the bits per symbol; η = k/2 b/s/Hz with rectangular pulses. For spectra, QPSK has the narrowest main lobe and MSK the lowest side lobes.

DSSS gains G<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>c</sub>/R<sub>b</sub> against narrowband interference, FHSS gains about the number of hop channels; the jamming margin subtracts the required E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>.

OFDM with Δf = 1/T<sub>u</sub> and a cyclic prefix at least as long as the delay spread turns a frequency-selective channel into flat subchannels; fading remains, so diversity and coding are still needed.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the generation and detection block diagram, the signal-space diagram and the error probability of each scheme, and many ask for a comparison of the schemes' spectra and bandwidth efficiency. Non-coherent BFSK and DPSK are often asked as one long question.

bank.q: Explain the generation and coherent detection of binary ASK (OOK) and binary FSK with block diagrams. State the decision rule of each, the role of the matched filter, and the bit error probability.
outline: OOK: unipolar NRZ times the carrier; BFSK: VCO or switched oscillators
OOK receiver: multiply by 2cos, integrate over T<sub>b</sub>, compare with A·T<sub>b</sub>/2
BFSK receiver: two correlators, decide by l<sub>1</sub> − l<sub>0</sub>
Matched filter h(t) = s(T<sub>b</sub> − t) equals the correlator at t = T<sub>b</sub> and maximises SNR
Signal space and P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) for both
answer: Signals. OOK sends s(t) = A cos(2πfc t) for a 1 and nothing for a 0, over 0 ≤ t < Tb. BFSK sends A cos(2πf1 t) for a 1 and A cos(2πf0 t) for a 0. With a 1 Ω reference, an OOK burst has energy A²Tb/2, so the average is Eb = A²Tb/4; every BFSK bit has Eb = A²Tb/2.

OOK generation. Turn the bits into a unipolar NRZ wave (1 → level 1, 0 → level 0) and multiply it by the carrier in a product modulator; a switch that passes or blocks the carrier is the simple version.

BFSK generation. Drive a voltage-controlled oscillator with the bipolar data so that it sits at f1 for a 1 and f0 for a 0; its phase is continuous. Switching between two oscillators also works but makes phase jumps that widen the spectrum.

answer.text: Coherent receivers. Top: OOK. Bottom: BFSK. Both need local carriers locked in frequency and phase to the received ones.

svg.aria: Block diagrams: the OOK receiver multiplies r of t by 2 cos of 2 pi f c t, integrates over one bit, samples and compares with A Tb over 2. The BFSK receiver has two branches, multiplying by cos at f1 and at f0, integrating, and comparing l1 minus l0 with zero.

answer: OOK decision rule. Without noise the integrator gives A·Tb for a 1 and 0 for a 0 (the factor 2 in the local carrier cancels the ½ of cos²). With equally likely bits and symmetric Gaussian noise the best threshold is the midpoint A·Tb/2: decide 1 if the sample exceeds it.

BFSK decision rule. The two correlator outputs l1 and l0 are compared: decide 1 if l1 − l0 > 0. For the f0 correlator to give nothing when f1 is sent, the tones must be orthogonal over a bit: spacing nRb/2 for a positive whole number n.

Matched filter. A filter with impulse response h(t) = s(Tb − t) gives, at t = Tb, exactly the correlator's output, because the convolution at that instant is ∫r(τ)s(τ)dτ. In white noise it maximises the output signal-to-noise ratio, which reaches 2E/N0 for a pulse of energy E. So the correlator and the matched filter are two ways of building the same optimum receiver.
Signal space. OOK points: 0 and √(2Eb) on one axis, d = √(2Eb). BFSK points: (√Eb, 0) and (0, √Eb), d = √(2Eb), boundary the 45° line.

answer.text: Error probability. For two points d apart in noise of density N0/2:
answer.pre: P<sub>b</sub> = Q(d/√(2N<sub>0</sub>)) = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>)/√(2N<sub>0</sub>)) = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>))

answer: This holds for both OOK (with the average E<sub>b</sub>) and orthogonal BFSK; both are 3 dB worse than BPSK.

answer.text: Numbers. Rb = 10 kb/s, f1 = 30 kHz, f0 = 20 kHz, Eb/N0 = 10 dB.

answer: Closing check. At the same peak amplitude BFSK has twice the Eb of OOK, so with A = 10 mV and N0 = 2.5 × 10−10 W/Hz OOK sits at 10 dB (7.83 × 10−4) and BFSK at 13 dB (Q(4.472) = 3.87 × 10−6). BFSK also needs no amplitude-dependent threshold.

bank.q: Define BPSK. Draw its signal-space diagram, describe its generation and coherent detection, and derive P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) for an AWGN channel. Evaluate P<sub>b</sub> at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 9.6 dB.
outline: Points ±√E<sub>b</sub> on the φ axis; boundary at 0
Balanced modulator; correlator with Costas or squaring loop
Correlator noise has variance N<sub>0</sub>/2; P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√E<sub>b</sub>/σ)
answer: Definition. BPSK sends s1(t) = √(2Eb/Tb)cos(2πfc t) for a 1 and s2(t) = −s1(t) for a 0, 0 ≤ t < Tb. The two waveforms are antipodal: same energy Eb, opposite sign, phases 0 and π.
Signal space. With the unit-energy basis φ(t) = √(2/Tb)cos(2πfc t), s1 = +√Eb·φ and s2 = −√Eb·φ: two points on one line, d = 2√Eb apart, with the decision boundary at zero.
Generation. Bits → bipolar NRZ (1 → +1, 0 → −1) → balanced modulator with the carrier √(2Eb/Tb)cos(2πfc t). The phase flips by 180° whenever the bit changes.
Detection. Multiply r(t) = s(t) + w(t) by φ(t), integrate over Tb, sample, and decide by the sign. The local carrier comes from a Costas or squaring loop, which locks with a 180° ambiguity.

answer.text: Statistics of the correlator output. w(t) is white Gaussian noise of two-sided density N0/2.
answer.pre:
y = ∫ r(t)φ(t) dt = ±√E<sub>b</sub> + n,   n = ∫ w(t)φ(t) dt
E[n] = 0
E[n²] = ∫∫ E[w(t)w(u)] φ(t)φ(u) dt du = (N<sub>0</sub>/2)∫ φ²(t) dt = N<sub>0</sub>/2

answer: So y is Gaussian with mean +√E<sub>b</sub> (bit 1) or −√E<sub>b</sub> (bit 0) and variance σ² = N<sub>0</sub>/2. With equal priors the maximum-likelihood threshold is midway, at 0.

answer.text: Error probability. A 1 is lost when n < −√Eb:
answer.pre:
P(e | 1) = P(n < −√E<sub>b</sub>) = Q(√E<sub>b</sub>/σ) = Q(√E<sub>b</sub>/√(N<sub>0</sub>/2)) = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>))
P(e | 0) = P(n > +√E<sub>b</sub>) = the same, by symmetry
P<sub>b</sub> = ½P(e | 1) + ½P(e | 0) = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) = ½erfc(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>))

svg.aria: Two bell curves centred at minus root Eb and plus root Eb with a dashed threshold at zero; the left tail of the bit-1 curve below zero is shaded as the error probability.

answer: Bandwidth. With rectangular bits the PSD is 2Eb·sinc²((f − fc)Tb): null-to-null 2Rb, efficiency 0.5 b/s/Hz, no carrier line because the bipolar data has zero mean.

Closing check. From distances, Pb = Q(d/√(2N0)) with d = 2√Eb gives Q(2√Eb/√(2N0)) = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), the same result. A 9.6 dB link therefore makes about one error in 100 000 bits, the usual design point quoted for BPSK.

bank.q: Compare coherent BFSK, non-coherent BFSK and DPSK. Describe the generation and detection of the two non-coherent schemes, state what carrier-phase information each receiver needs, and compare their error probabilities at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB.
outline: Coherent BFSK: two correlators with locked carriers
Non-coherent BFSK: bandpass filters and envelope detectors; spacing ≥ R<sub>b</sub>
DPSK: differential encoder and BPSK modulator; delay-and-multiply receiver
Values at 10 dB and the required E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> for 10<sup>−5</sup>
answer: Coherent BFSK. Two correlators, at f1 and f0, each with a local carrier locked in frequency and phase; decide by l1 − l0. Tone spacing nRb/2. Pb = Q(√(Eb/N0)).

Non-coherent BFSK, generation. The same as coherent BFSK: a VCO or switched oscillators. Only the receiver changes, but the tones must now be spaced by a whole multiple of Rb, because they must be orthogonal for every phase difference.

Non-coherent BFSK, detection. Two bandpass filters centred on f1 and f0, each followed by an envelope detector (or, equivalently, I and Q correlators at each tone whose outputs are squared and added). Sample both envelopes at the end of the bit; the larger wins. The envelope does not depend on the carrier phase, so no phase reference is needed; only the bit timing and the two frequencies. Pb = ½e−Eb/2N0.

answer.text: DPSK, generation. A differential encoder dk = bk ⊕ dk−1 (with a known reference d0) feeds a BPSK modulator: dk = 1 → phase π, dk = 0 → phase 0. A data 1 therefore flips the phase and a data 0 keeps it.

answer: DPSK, detection. Multiply the received signal by a copy delayed by Tb and integrate over the bit (the optimum form correlates the I and Q outputs of successive bits). A negative result means a phase change, so bk = 1. The receiver needs no absolute phase, only a phase that stays steady over two bits; a constant offset, even 180°, cancels. Pb = ½e−Eb/N0, exact for this receiver.

Reading the table. Dropping the phase reference costs about 0.75 dB at 10−5 in both families (10.34 − 9.59 and 13.35 − 12.60). Orthogonal FSK costs 3 dB against antipodal PSK in both. DPSK is the best scheme that needs no carrier recovery.

Where each fits. Coherent BFSK: rarely worth the carrier loop, since BPSK is 3 dB better. Non-coherent BFSK: cheap telemetry, pagers, sensor links. DPSK: links whose phase drifts slowly; it fails if the phase moves noticeably within two bits, and its errors tend to come in pairs.
Closing check. At 12 dB the same order holds: 9.0 × 10−9, 6.5 × 10−8, 3.4 × 10−5 and 1.8 × 10−4, and the non-coherent penalties shrink as the signal grows.

bank.q: Describe QPSK generation and coherent detection with block diagrams. Find the transmitted phases for the bits 1 0 0 1 1 1, and explain why Gray-coded QPSK has the same bit error probability as BPSK at the same E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. Take R<sub>b</sub> = 2 Mb/s and E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 9.6 dB.
outline: s(t) = A[I cos − Q sin], I, Q = ±1, T<sub>s</sub> = 2T<sub>b</sub>
Each branch is BPSK with energy E<sub>b</sub>: P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) = 9.74 × 10<sup>−6</sup>
answer: Signal. s(t) = A[I cos(2πfc t) − Q sin(2πfc t)], 0 ≤ t < Ts, with I, Q = ±1. The phase is arctan(Q/I) and the symbol energy Es = A²Ts = 2Eb.

Transmitter. (1) A serial-to-parallel converter sends odd-numbered bits to the I branch and even-numbered bits to the Q branch. (2) Each branch makes bipolar NRZ at Rs = Rb/2. (3) Balanced modulators multiply I by cos(2πfc t) and Q by −sin(2πfc t). (4) An adder combines them.

Receiver. A carrier-recovery loop gives cos and −sin. Two correlators multiply r(t) by each and integrate over Ts; the sign of the I output gives the first bit and the sign of the Q output the second; a parallel-to-serial converter restores the order.

answer.text: Phases for 1 0 0 1 1 1 (pairs 10, 01, 11; first bit → I, second → Q, 1 → +1):

answer: So the carrier sits at 315° for the first symbol, jumps by 180° to 135°, then by −90° to 45°. Each symbol lasts T<sub>s</sub> = 2T<sub>b</sub> = 1 µs at R<sub>b</sub> = 2 Mb/s.
Gray labels. The four points 11 (45°), 01 (135°), 00 (225°), 10 (315°) put one-bit differences between neighbours, so the likeliest symbol error (to a neighbour) costs one bit.

answer.text: Why Pb equals BPSK. Insert s(t) into the I correlator:
answer.pre: ∫ [A·I cos − A·Q sin]·cos dt over T<sub>s</sub> = A·I·T<sub>s</sub>/2 − A·Q·(0) = A·I·T<sub>s</sub>/2

answer: The Q term integrates to zero because cos and sin are orthogonal over a symbol, so the I decision sees only its own bit plus noise, exactly a BPSK detector with energy E<sub>s</sub>/2 = E<sub>b</sub> per bit. The same holds for Q. Hence P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)).

answer.pre:
R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 1 Msymbol/s;  B = 2R<sub>s</sub> = 2 MHz (BPSK would need 4 MHz)
E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10<sup>0.96</sup> = 9.120;  √(2 × 9.120) = 4.271
P<sub>b</sub> = Q(4.271) = 9.74 × 10<sup>−6</sup>;  P<sub>s</sub> = 2P<sub>b</sub> − P<sub>b</sub>² = 1.95 × 10<sup>−5</sup>

answer: Phase error. A carrier error θ rotates the constellation: the I output becomes A(I cos θ − Q sin θ)Ts/2, so the bits leak into each other and the margin shrinks; that is why QPSK needs a good carrier loop.
Closing check. 2 Mb/s in 2 MHz is 1 b/s/Hz, twice BPSK's 0.5, at the same 9.74 × 10−6 bit error rate: QPSK doubles the bandwidth efficiency at no cost in power.

bank.q: Compare the power spectral densities of BPSK, QPSK and MSK. Write their expressions, sketch them, and compare main-lobe width, side lobes and 99% bandwidth at R<sub>b</sub> = 10 kb/s. Which suits a crowded band, and why?
outline: MSK for crowded bands and saturating amplifiers

answer.text: Expressions (complex-envelope PSDs, f measured from the carrier, same Eb and Rb = 1/Tb; sinc x = sin πx/πx):
answer.pre:
BPSK:  S(f) = 2E<sub>b</sub> sinc²(fT<sub>b</sub>)
QPSK:  S(f) = 4E<sub>b</sub> sinc²(2fT<sub>b</sub>)
MSK:   S(f) = (32E<sub>b</sub>/π²) [cos(2πfT<sub>b</sub>)/(16f²T<sub>b</sub>² − 1)]²

answer: Where they come from. BPSK uses rectangular pulses of length Tb, whose spectrum is a sinc. QPSK uses rectangular pulses of length 2Tb on two rails, so its sinc is twice as narrow and its peak twice as high. MSK uses half-sine pulses of length 2Tb; a smooth pulse has a spectrum that falls faster.

svg.aria: Three curves of power spectral density against frequency from the carrier, 0 to 2 bit rates: QPSK with the tallest, narrowest main lobe ending at 0.5, MSK ending at 0.75, BPSK ending at 1.

head: BPSK
QPSK
MSK
rows: Level at 2.5R<sub>b</sub> from f<sub>c</sub> (vs BPSK peak)

answer: How the numbers were found. The nulls are where the sinc or the cosine vanish (MSK: cos 2πfTb = 0 at fTb = 0.75, the zero at 0.25 being cancelled by the denominator). The side-lobe levels are the first local maxima, at fTb ≈ 1.43 (BPSK), 0.715 (QPSK) and 0.945 (MSK). The 99% bands come from integrating each PSD until 99% of the total power is enclosed.
BFSK for reference. Ordinary BFSK with h = 1 needs a Carson band of 2(Δf + Rb) = 30 kHz at 10 kb/s, and with phase jumps its side lobes fall only as 1/f².

Which suits a crowded band. QPSK has the narrowest main lobe, but its side lobes are as high as BPSK's, so it leaks into neighbouring channels unless filtered, and filtering gives it a varying envelope that a saturating amplifier distorts. MSK's main lobe is wider, but 99% of its power sits within about 1.2Rb and it keeps a constant envelope. That is why MSK, and GMSK with even lower side lobes, were chosen for crowded mobile bands such as GSM.

Closing check. All three spectra carry the same total power Eb/Tb per side: for BPSK ∫2Eb sinc²(fTb)df = 2Eb/Tb over both sides, and the QPSK and MSK expressions integrate to the same 2Eb/Tb, as they must for the same bit energy and rate.

bank.q: A BPSK link has E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 8 dB at R<sub>b</sub> = 1 Mb/s. Find P<sub>b</sub> and the expected errors per second. If the same link used OOK with the same average bit energy, find its P<sub>b</sub> and the extra E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> OOK would need to match BPSK.
outline: OOK needs 2 × 6.31 = 12.62, which is 11.0 dB: 3 dB more
answer: Given. Eb/N0 = 8 dB, Rb = 106 bit/s. BPSK: Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)). Coherent OOK with average Eb: Pb = Q(√(Eb/N0)).
Errors per second. 106 × 1.91 × 10−4 = 191 errors/s on average, about one in every 5240 bits.
That is about 31 times worse than BPSK: 6000 errors/s at 1 Mb/s.
Why. BPSK's points ±√Eb are d = 2√Eb apart; OOK's points 0 and √(2Eb) are only √(2Eb) apart. The ratio of squared distances is 4Eb/2Eb = 2, which is 3 dB.
Threshold note. The OOK receiver also needs its threshold at half the received burst amplitude, which must be tracked as the signal level changes; BPSK's threshold is always zero.
Closing check. Doubling OOK's Eb/N0 from 6.31 to 12.62 makes its Q argument √12.62 = 3.552, exactly BPSK's, so the two give the same 1.91 × 10−4: the 3 dB gap is exact.

bank.q: Design a Gray-coded 16-QAM constellation with levels ±a, ±3a. Find the bits per symbol, the average symbol energy, d<sub>min</sub> and the bandwidth efficiency. Compare d<sub>min</sub> with 16-PSK of the same average energy, and both symbol error probabilities at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 12 dB.
answer: Bits. k = log2 16 = 4 bits per symbol: the first two choose I, the last two choose Q.

answer.text: Gray mapping per axis: 00 → −3a, 01 → −a, 11 → +a, 10 → +3a (neighbouring levels differ in one bit). The grid, written as I-bits Q-bits:

answer: Every horizontal or vertical neighbour differs in exactly one bit, so a symbol error to a neighbour costs one bit.

answer.text: Average energy. Each axis takes ±a and ±3a equally often:
answer.pre:
E[I²] = (a² + a² + 9a² + 9a²)/4 = 5a²,  E[Q²] = 5a²
E<sub>s</sub> = E[I²] + E[Q²] = 10a²  (formula 2(M − 1)a²/3 = 2 × 15/3 a² = 10a²)
E<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>s</sub>/4 = 2.5a²

answer: Minimum distance. Neighbours are 2a apart: dmin = 2a = 2√(Es/10) = 0.632√Es, and dmin² = 4a² = 1.6Eb.
Bandwidth efficiency. Rs = Rb/4. With rectangular pulses B = 2Rs, η = 4/2 = 2 b/s/Hz; with ideal Nyquist pulses B = Rs, η = 4 b/s/Hz. Receiver thresholds sit at −2a, 0 and +2a on each axis.
16-QAM keeps its points 1.62 times further apart, worth 4.2 dB: points spread over a square use the plane better than points on a circle.

Conclusion. Same bits per symbol, same bandwidth, but 16-PSK makes about 50 times more symbol errors at 12 dB. 16-PSK's only advantage is its constant amplitude, which matters only with a strongly nonlinear amplifier.

Closing check. 4.2 dB of distance should shift the 16-PSK curve right by about 4.2 dB: at 10−5 bit error, 16-QAM needs about 13.4 dB and 16-PSK about 17.4 dB, a 4.0 dB gap, close to the distance estimate.

bank.q: An OFDM system has 64 subcarriers and a useful symbol time of 3.2 µs. Find the subcarrier spacing and choose a cyclic prefix for a channel delay spread of 0.8 µs. With 48 data subcarriers carrying 16-QAM, find the overhead and the bit rate. What changes if the delay spread grows to 1.2 µs?
outline: 1.2 µs: T = 4.4 µs, overhead 27.3%, 43.6 Mb/s; or double N to cut the overhead

answer.pre:
Δf = 1/T<sub>u</sub> = 1/3.2 µs = 312.5 kHz
B = N·Δf = 64 × 312.5 kHz = 20 MHz;  sample time 1/B = 50 ns

answer: Prefix. The prefix must be at least the delay spread: Tcp ≥ 0.8 µs. Take Tcp = 0.8 µs = 16 samples. Then T = Tu + Tcp = 4.0 µs.
Overhead. Tcp/T = 0.8/4.0 = 20% of the air time carries no new data.

answer.pre:
bits per OFDM symbol = 48 × log<sub>2</sub> 16 = 48 × 4 = 192
R = 192/4.0 µs = 48 Mb/s  (uncoded)

answer: Why it works. The 0.8 µs of echo from the previous symbol lands inside the prefix, which the receiver throws away; the kept 3.2 µs block is a circular convolution of the data with the channel, so the FFT gives Y[k] = H[k]X[k] + W[k] and each subcarrier needs one complex division.

answer.pre:
T<sub>cp</sub> = 1.2 µs (24 samples);  T = 4.4 µs
overhead = 1.2/4.4 = 27.3%
R = 192/4.4 µs = 43.6 Mb/s

answer: Better alternative. Keep the 20 MHz band but use N = 128: Δf = 156.25 kHz, Tu = 6.4 µs, T = 7.6 µs, overhead 1.2/7.6 = 15.8%. With 96 data subcarriers the rate is 96 × 4/7.6 µs = 50.5 Mb/s. The cost: subcarriers twice as close are twice as sensitive to frequency offset and Doppler.
If the prefix were left at 0.8 µs. The last 0.4 µs of echo would fall inside the FFT window, giving intersymbol and inter-carrier interference that no one-tap equaliser can remove.
Closing check. 312.5 kHz × 3.2 µs = 1: each subcarrier makes a whole number of cycles in Tu, which is the orthogonality condition.

bank.q: A DSSS system uses 127 chips per bit with BPSK at R<sub>b</sub> = 10 kb/s. Find the processing gain, the chip rate and the transmitted bandwidth. How is a 127-chip code made? If the receiver needs E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 9.6 dB and has 2 dB of losses, find the jamming margin, and explain how spreading defeats a narrowband interferer.
outline: Despreading spreads the interferer; only 1/G<sub>p</sub> remains in the data band

answer.pre:
G<sub>p</sub> = chips per bit = 127
G<sub>p</sub>(dB) = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 127 = 21.04 dB

answer: Chip rate and bandwidth. Rc = Gp × Rb = 127 × 10 kb/s = 1.27 Mchip/s. The BPSK main lobe is 2Rc = 2.54 MHz wide, against 2Rb = 20 kHz for the unspread signal: 127 times wider.

The code. 127 = 2⁷ − 1, the period of a maximal-length sequence from a 7-stage shift register with suitable XOR feedback. It has 64 ones and 63 zeros (balance), the run property, and an autocorrelation of 127 at zero shift and −1 at every other shift, so the receiver can find and track the code phase.

answer.pre:
M<sub>j</sub> = G<sub>p</sub>(dB) − (E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)<sub>req</sub> − L<sub>sys</sub> = 21.04 − 9.6 − 2 = 9.44 dB
J/S allowed = 10<sup>0.944</sup> = 8.8

answer: A jammer may arrive up to 8.8 times stronger than the wanted signal and the link still meets its target (about 10<sup>−5</sup> for BPSK at 9.6 dB).

How spreading defeats a narrowband interferer. (1) The transmitter multiplies the data by the code, spreading it over 2.54 MHz. (2) The interferer is added in the channel, still narrow. (3) The receiver multiplies by the same code: the wanted signal collapses back to 20 kHz (c² = 1), while the interferer, multiplied by the code for the first time, is spread over 2.54 MHz. (4) The data filter or correlator keeps about 1/Gp = 1/127 of the interferer's power.
Limits. A wideband jammer that fills the whole 2.54 MHz is not reduced by despreading. Code timing must be held within a fraction of a chip (0.79 µs here).

Closing check. After despreading the interferer's in-band power drops by 21.04 dB; with J/S = 8.8 (9.44 dB) the in-band ratio becomes 9.44 − 21.04 = −11.6 dB, and adding the 2 dB loss and the 9.6 dB requirement accounts for the whole 21.04 dB: 9.44 + 9.6 + 2 = 21.04.

bank.q: An MSK transmitter sends R<sub>b</sub> = 200 kb/s on a 900 MHz carrier. Find the two frequencies, the tone spacing and the modulation index. Draw up the phase trellis for the data 1 0 0 1 1 1 0, find the main-lobe and 99% bandwidths and P<sub>b</sub> at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB. If it is turned into GMSK with BT = 0.3, find the Gaussian filter bandwidth and state the trade-off.
outline: f = 900 MHz ± 50 kHz; spacing 100 kHz; h = 0.5
GMSK B = 60 kHz: narrower spectrum, more ISI

answer.pre:
Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/4 = 50 kHz
f<sub>1</sub> = 900 MHz + 50 kHz = 900.05 MHz  (bit 1)
f<sub>2</sub> = 900 MHz − 50 kHz = 899.95 MHz  (bit 0)
spacing = 100 kHz = R<sub>b</sub>/2;  h = 100/200 = 0.5

answer: Why this spacing. Rb/2 is the smallest spacing at which two tones are coherently orthogonal over a bit, which is where the name minimum shift keying comes from.

answer.text: Phase trellis. Each 1 adds 2π(Rb/4)Tb = π/2 and each 0 subtracts π/2, starting from θ = 0:

answer: The phase moves in straight 5 µs ramps (T<sub>b</sub> = 1/200 kHz) and never jumps, so the envelope is constant.
Bandwidths. Main lobe 1.5Rb = 300 kHz between nulls. 99% power bandwidth about 1.18Rb = 236 kHz. (QPSK at the same rate: main lobe 200 kHz but 99% band about 2 MHz.)

answer.text: Error probability. Coherent MSK detects each I and Q rail over 2Tb with energy Eb per bit, like QPSK:

answer: GMSK. B = BT × Rb = 0.3 × 200 kHz = 60 kHz for the Gaussian lowpass filter placed before the frequency modulator.

Trade-off. The Gaussian filter rounds the frequency steps, so the spectrum gets narrower and the side lobes much lower: good for adjacent channels. But each bit's frequency change now spreads over about three bit times, so neighbouring bits interfere (ISI); a simple detector loses some dB, and a Viterbi equaliser is used to win most of it back. The envelope stays constant either way because the filter acts on the data, not on the RF signal.
Closing check. Over the seven bits there are four 1s and three 0s, so the final phase is (4 − 3) × 90° = 90°, as in the table.

bank.q: Compare BPSK, QPSK, 16-PSK and 16-QAM at equal E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB: bits per symbol, bandwidth efficiency, minimum distance and bit error probability. Which would you choose for a power-limited link and which for a bandwidth-limited one?
outline: Power-limited: BPSK or QPSK; bandwidth-limited: 16-QAM, never 16-PSK
answer: Common basis. Same Eb/N0 = 10 (10 dB), Gray labels, rectangular pulses so η = k/2.

answer.pre:
BPSK:   d² = (2√E<sub>b</sub>)² = 4E<sub>b</sub>
QPSK:   d² = 2E<sub>s</sub> = 4E<sub>b</sub>  (E<sub>s</sub> = 2E<sub>b</sub>)
16-PSK: d² = 4E<sub>s</sub> sin²(π/16) = 16E<sub>b</sub> × 0.03806 = 0.609E<sub>b</sub>
16-QAM: d² = 4a² with E<sub>s</sub> = 10a² = 4E<sub>b</sub>  ⇒  d² = 1.6E<sub>b</sub>

answer: Reading it. QPSK doubles BPSK's efficiency for free, because it uses the second (quadrature) dimension. Going to 16 points doubles η again but costs power: 3.8 dB for 16-QAM and 7.8 dB for 16-PSK at 10−5. 16-PSK loses to 16-QAM because its points are confined to a circle.
Spectra. All four have sinc² spectra with rectangular pulses; at a fixed bit rate the main lobe is 2Rb/k: 2Rb, Rb, Rb/2, Rb/2.
Power-limited link (satellite, deep space, battery sensor): BPSK or QPSK. QPSK gives the same Pb with half the bandwidth, so it is usually preferred if the carrier recovery is good.

Bandwidth-limited link (cable, microwave backhaul, Wi-Fi near the router): 16-QAM, provided the SNR is about 4 dB higher and the amplifier is linear. 16-PSK has no reason to be chosen except with a hard-limiting amplifier.

Closing check. The distance estimate 10 log(4/1.6) = 4.0 dB matches the 13.4 − 9.6 = 3.8 dB gap at 10−5 closely; 10 log(4/0.609) = 8.2 dB matches 17.4 − 9.6 = 7.8 dB. The small differences come from the neighbour counts.

bank.q: A 20 MHz channel has a delay spread of 5 µs. Compare a single-carrier QAM link at 20 Msymbol/s with an OFDM link in the same band: intersymbol interference, equalisation effort, cyclic-prefix overhead, peak-to-average power and synchronisation. Which would you choose?
outline: Single carrier: 5 µs × 20 Msymbol/s = 100 symbols of ISI; long equaliser
OFDM with N = 1024: Δf = 19.53 kHz, T<sub>u</sub> = 51.2 µs, T<sub>cp</sub> = 5 µs, overhead 8.9%
One complex division per subcarrier after a 1024-point FFT
OFDM: high PAPR, sensitive to frequency offset
answer: Single carrier. Symbol time 1/20 MHz = 50 ns. The echoes last 5 µs, so each received sample mixes 5 µs × 20 × 106 = 100 symbols. The channel is strongly frequency-selective (coherence bandwidth about 1/(5στ); with στ ≈ 1 µs that is roughly 200 kHz, a hundredth of the band).

Single-carrier equalisation. A time-domain equaliser needs at least about 100 taps, often several hundred, each a complex multiply per symbol, and it must adapt as the channel changes; a maximum-likelihood sequence detector would be far too complex for 16-QAM over 100 symbols.

answer.text: OFDM design. Pick the prefix first, then make Tu long enough that the prefix is a small overhead:

answer: N = 1024 is a reasonable choice: 8.9% overhead, and a 19.5 kHz subcarrier is much narrower than the coherence bandwidth, so each sees flat fading.

OFDM equalisation. A 1024-point FFT costs about (N/2)log2 N = 5120 complex multiplies per OFDM symbol, about 5 per subcarrier, plus one complex division per subcarrier: roughly 6 operations per data symbol instead of 100 or more.

Peak-to-average power. With 1024 subcarriers adding with random phases the signal looks Gaussian; rare peaks far above the mean force the amplifier to back off several dB, costing power efficiency. Single-carrier 16-QAM has a much lower PAPR (2.55 dB for the constellation itself: peak 18a² over average 10a²).

Synchronisation. OFDM subcarriers 19.5 kHz apart lose orthogonality if the carrier is off by a noticeable fraction of that. A 2 GHz oscillator with 2 ppm error is 4 kHz off, 20% of Δf, so OFDM needs frequency-offset estimation and correction; Doppler at 30 m/s (200 Hz) is only 1% of Δf. Timing is relaxed by the prefix.
Fading still matters. OFDM removes the ISI but some subcarriers fall into deep notches; coding and interleaving across subcarriers turn the frequency selectivity into diversity.

Verdict. For a 100-symbol delay spread OFDM wins clearly on equaliser complexity, at the cost of 9% overhead, a linear amplifier with back-off, and careful frequency synchronisation. That is the choice made by Wi-Fi, LTE and DVB-T. Single carrier (with frequency-domain equalisation) remains attractive for uplinks where amplifier efficiency matters, which is why LTE uses DFT-spread OFDM there.
Closing check. 1/19.53 kHz = 51.2 µs and 5/(51.2 + 5) = 0.089, consistent with the table.

bank.q: Compare DSSS and FHSS for interference rejection and multiple access when both spread a 10 kb/s signal over 25 MHz. Include processing gain, chip rate, hop rate and the near-far problem.
outline: FHSS: 1000 channels of 25 kHz, G<sub>p</sub> ≈ 1000 (30 dB)
Narrowband jammer: DSSS spreads it; FHSS avoids it most of the time
CDMA by codes vs by hop patterns
Near-far: 40 dB for a 10× distance ratio; DSSS needs power control, FHSS suffers only collisions

answer.text: DSSS numbers. To fill about 25 MHz with BPSK chips the main lobe 2Rc must be 25 MHz:
answer.pre: R<sub>c</sub> = 12.5 Mchip/s;  G<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>c</sub>/R<sub>b</sub> = 12.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>/10<sup>4</sup> = 1250  →  30.97 dB

answer.text: FHSS numbers. With BFSK in 25 kHz channels:
answer.pre:
N = 25 MHz/25 kHz = 1000 channels;  G<sub>p</sub> ≈ 1000  →  30.0 dB
slow hopping at 1000 hops/s: 10 bits per hop
fast hopping at 4 hops/bit: 40 000 hops/s, 25 µs dwell

answer: Processing gain. Almost the same, about 30 dB, because both occupy the same total band for the same data rate.

Against a narrowband jammer. DSSS: the receiver's code multiplication spreads the jammer over 25 MHz, leaving about 1/1250 of its power in the data band, all the time. FHSS: the radio lands on the jammed channel 1 hop in 1000; that hop may be lost, but coding and interleaving repair it. A partial-band jammer covering 10% of the band hits 10% of FHSS hops but is spread just as well by DSSS.

Against a follower jammer. FHSS with fast hopping leaves each channel in 25 µs, before a jammer can measure and follow. DSSS has no such weakness, but it has no way to avoid a strong wideband jammer either.

Multiple access. DSSS-CDMA: each user has its own code; others appear as noise reduced by Gp, so capacity falls gently as users are added. FH multiple access: each user has its own hop pattern; two users collide only when they land on the same channel in the same dwell, probability about 1/1000 per hop per interfering user.

answer.text: Near-far problem. With a path-loss exponent of 4, a user 10 times closer is 40 dB stronger:
answer.pre: 10 log(10<sup>4</sup>) = 40 dB  >  G<sub>p</sub> = 31 dB

answer: In DSSS that near user swamps the far one, since despreading suppresses it by only 31 dB; tight power control (as in CDMA mobiles) is essential. In FHSS the near user hurts only when the two collide on a channel, so the problem is much milder.
Practical cost. DSSS needs chip-level synchronisation (80 ns chips) and a 25 MHz-wide front end; FHSS needs a fast-settling synthesiser and only a 25 kHz-wide receiver at any instant.

Verdict. DSSS suits cellular CDMA and GPS, where power control and precise timing are available and steady suppression of everything else is wanted. FHSS suits military radios and Bluetooth, where avoiding interference and tolerating strong nearby users matter more.
Closing check. 12.5 Mchip/s / 10 kb/s = 1250 and 25 MHz / 25 kHz = 1000: the two gains differ by 10 log 1.25 = 0.97 dB, so the comparison is fair.

bank.q: Evaluate the claim: "Higher-order QAM always improves performance because it sends more bits per symbol." Use a 10 MHz channel (B = 2R<sub>s</sub>) with a fixed received S/N<sub>0</sub> that gives E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 12 dB for QPSK, and compare QPSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM.
outline: More bits per symbol cost power; the claim is false when SNR is limited
Adaptive modulation picks M from the measured SNR
answer: Bit rates. Rs = B/2 = 5 Msymbol/s for all three. QPSK 2 × 5 = 10 Mb/s; 16-QAM 20 Mb/s; 64-QAM 30 Mb/s. So far the claim looks right.

answer.text: Fixed received power. The transmitter and the path set S/N0, not Eb/N0:
answer.pre:
S/N<sub>0</sub> = (E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)·R<sub>b</sub> = 15.85 × 10<sup>7</sup> = 1.585 × 10<sup>8</sup> Hz  (82.0 dB-Hz)
E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = (S/N<sub>0</sub>)/R<sub>b</sub>:  QPSK 15.85 (12.0 dB), 16-QAM 7.92 (9.0 dB), 64-QAM 5.28 (7.2 dB)

answer: Every extra bit per symbol spreads the same energy over more bits, so E<sub>b</sub> falls.

Evaluation. At this SNR 64-QAM makes an error in about every 16th bit, useless even with strong coding; 16-QAM's 4.4 × 10−3 needs heavy coding that eats much of its rate gain; QPSK is nearly error-free. So the claim is false: higher order raises the bandwidth efficiency but lowers the power efficiency, and it pays only when the SNR is high enough.

When it is true. If S/N0 rises by about 10.6 dB (to 92.6 dB-Hz, a phone close to the router), 64-QAM reaches its 17.8 dB at 30 Mb/s and triples the throughput in the same band. That is why real systems use adaptive modulation: they measure the SNR and choose QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM or higher accordingly.

Other limits. Higher-order QAM also needs a more linear amplifier (higher peak-to-average power), a cleaner oscillator (phase noise rotates closely spaced points across boundaries) and finer converters.
Closing check. Eb/N0 falls by 10 log 2 = 3.0 dB from QPSK to 16-QAM and by 10 log 1.5 = 1.8 dB more to 64-QAM, matching 12.0 → 9.0 → 7.2 dB.

glossary.def: A signal whose spectrum sits around a carrier frequency f<sub>c</sub> rather than around zero.
One waveform chosen from a finite set and sent for T<sub>s</sub> seconds; it carries k = log<sub>2</sub> M bits.
Additive white Gaussian noise, with power spectral density N<sub>0</sub>/2 at all frequencies.
Detection with a local carrier locked in frequency and phase to the received one.
Detection that does not need the carrier phase, using envelopes or phase differences.
Multiplies the received signal by a reference waveform and integrates over a symbol; equivalent to a matched filter sampled at the symbol end.
A filter with impulse response s(T − t); it maximises the output signal-to-noise ratio at t = T in white noise.
A circuit that outputs the slowly varying amplitude of a bandpass signal.
Two signals that are negatives of each other, such as the two BPSK waveforms.
Signals whose product integrates to zero over a symbol.
A bit mapping in which neighbouring constellation points differ in one bit.
The set of symbol points plotted in signal space.
The set of received points nearer to one constellation point than to any other.
Energy per bit over one-sided noise density; the fair measure for comparing schemes.
h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub>, the tone spacing divided by the bit rate; 0.5 for MSK.
FSK whose phase does not jump at bit boundaries.
The Gaussian filter's 3 dB bandwidth times the bit time in GMSK.
One bit of a spreading code, of duration T<sub>c</sub>.
A deterministic binary sequence with noise-like properties, made by a shift register with feedback.
The spreading factor of a spread-spectrum system: chips per bit in DSSS, hop channels in FHSS.
In CDMA, a strong nearby user swamping a weak distant one; cured by power control.
The time between the first and last significant echoes of a multipath channel.
The frequency range over which the channel gain stays nearly constant.
The time over which the channel gain stays nearly constant.
Fading of a channel with many scattered paths and no direct one; the amplitude follows a Rayleigh distribution.
Sending or receiving a symbol over independently fading paths, then combining them.
One of the many narrowband carriers of an OFDM symbol.
A copy of the end of an OFDM symbol placed before it to absorb echoes.
Peak-to-average power ratio; high in OFDM and QAM, it forces the amplifier to back off.
